summary: This document specifies how SCTP can run on top of DTLS. SCTP itself does not know about the encryption, so the combination protects SCTP packets and can pass through places where plain SCTP would not work. It is used for WebRTC data channels.

eli5.summary: It puts SCTP packets in a sealed envelope before sending, so they travel privately and the post office does not need to understand what is inside.

questions: how to run sctp over dtls
why can sctp over dtls only be single-homed
what path mtu should sctp over dtls use
subtitle: How to carry SCTP packets inside DTLS, so SCTP gets encryption and NAT-friendly transport without knowing what is underneath.

tldr.problem: SCTP was defined to run directly on IPv4 or IPv6. Some uses, such as moving non-SRTP data between browsers, need SCTP to run over a secure, NAT-friendly datagram layer instead.
tldr.mechanism: Each complete SCTP packet (common header plus chunks) is handed to DTLS as application data, and the receiving DTLS layer passes the payload back up to SCTP. SCTP is unaware of anything below DTLS, so it has no IP addresses to work with.
tldr.outcome: The stack gives confidentiality, source authentication and integrity, and can help with NAT traversal. The price is that SCTP associations over DTLS can only be single-homed. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8899 and RFC 8996.

sections.title: Overview of the Encapsulation
sections.content:
The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) normally runs on top of IPv4 or IPv6. RFC 8261 specifies how to run it on top of Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) instead. The stack is SCTP on DTLS on ICE/UDP, and the RFC names the WebRTC protocol suite as an example user: it transports non-SRTP data between browsers this way.

Running over DTLS over UDP or ICE/UDP can provide a NAT traversal solution in addition to confidentiality, source authentication and integrity-protected transfers. Using ICE does not necessarily mean a different packet format is used on the wire.

The procedures in RFC 6951 for dealing with UDP port numbers do not apply here. With this encapsulation, SCTP is unaware of the protocols used below DTLS.
sections.eli5: SCTP is like a letter writer who hands every letter to a secure courier service. The writer does not care which roads the courier uses.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
sections.content:
The procedure is deliberately simple. When SCTP gives a packet to the DTLS layer, the complete SCTP packet, made of the SCTP common header and a number of chunks, is treated as the payload of the DTLS application-layer protocol.

When the DTLS layer has processed a DTLS record that carries an application-layer message, it passes the payload to SCTP. SCTP expects to see an SCTP common header followed by a number of chunks.
sections.eli5: Put the whole SCTP packet in the envelope on the way out. Take it out of the envelope on the way in.

sections.title: Path MTU, Fragmentation and DTLS Requirements
sections.content:
An implementation MUST implement and use a path MTU discovery method that works without ICMP. An implementation of Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (RFC 4821), in either SCTP or DTLS, is RECOMMENDED. When SCTP over DTLS is used for WebRTC data channels, path MTU discovery is performed by SCTP.

The DTLS implementation MUST support DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) and SHOULD support the newest published version, which was DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) at publication time. Because SCTP does its own segmentation and reassembly based on the path MTU, the DTLS layer MUST NOT use any compression algorithm. DTLS MUST also support sending messages larger than the current path MTU, which might result in IP-level fragmentation.

If DTLS performs path MTU discovery, it MUST use the method of RFC 4821, with the extension from RFC 6520 for probe packets. If SCTP performs it over IPv4, DTLS SHOULD let its user set the Don't Fragment bit. If that is impossible, SCTP has to use a safe path MTU value, and it is RECOMMENDED not to exceed 1200 bytes.

The RFC points out that RFC 1122 only requires end hosts to reassemble fragmented IP packets up to 576 bytes.
sections.eli5: Big packages may need to be cut up, and SCTP does the cutting, so the envelope must not squash them. If the sender cannot be sure how big a package fits, it plays safe and sends smaller ones.

sections.title: DSCP and ECN Pass-Through
sections.content:
The DTLS implementation SHOULD let its user set the Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) on outgoing IP packets. That needs DTLS to pass the value through and the lower layer to allow setting it. If it cannot, the default of the protocol stack is used. Only a single DSCP value can be used for all packets of one SCTP association.

Using Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) in SCTP requires DTLS to pass the ECN bits through and its lower layer to expose them for sent and received packets. If that is not possible, ECN cannot be used by SCTP.
sections.eli5: SCTP sometimes wants to put a priority sticker or a traffic-jam warning on a package. The envelope service has to let those stickers show through, or SCTP goes without.

sections.title: Restrictions on Base SCTP
sections.content:
SCTP as defined in RFC 4960 is used with restrictions that reflect DTLS being the lower layer:

  • A DTLS connection MUST be established before an SCTP association is set up.
  • Multiple SCTP associations MAY be multiplexed over one DTLS connection, using SCTP port numbers to multiplex and demultiplex.
  • All associations are single-homed, because DTLS exposes no address management. It is RECOMMENDED to set path.max.retrans to association.max.retrans.
  • INIT and INIT-ACK chunks MUST NOT contain IPv4 Address or IPv6 Address parameters, and INIT MUST NOT contain the Supported Address Types parameter.
  • The implementation MUST NOT rely on processing ICMP or ICMPv6 packets.
  • If SCTP is told of a path change, it SHOULD retest the path MTU and reset congestion state to the initial state.
sections.eli5: Because SCTP cannot see the real addresses, it cannot use several roads at once and must not mention addresses at all. It also must not count on warning notes from the road network.

sections.title: SCTP Extensions That Work Over DTLS
sections.content:
The RFC goes through the main SCTP extensions:

  • Padding (RFC 4820): when SCTP does path MTU discovery, this MUST be supported and used for probes, which are HEARTBEAT chunks bundled with PADDING chunks.
  • Dynamic address reconfiguration (RFC 5061): if used, ASCONF chunks MUST use wildcard addresses only.
  • Authentication (RFC 4895): can be used, but gives no additional benefit.
  • Partial reliability (RFC 3758): can be used, as can extra policies such as those in RFC 7496.
  • Stream reset (RFC 6525): can be used to reset and add streams during an association.
  • Interleaving of large user messages (RFC 8260): can be used and overcomes a limit of base SCTP.
sections.eli5: SCTP has optional add-on features. Most of them still work inside the envelope. The address-changing one only works in a limited, wildcard form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations for DTLS are in RFC 4347 and for SCTP in RFC 4960, RFC 3758 and RFC 6525. The RFC states that combining SCTP and DTLS introduces no new security considerations.

SCTP should not process the IP addresses used for the underlying communication, since DTLS provides no guarantees about them. The inability to process ICMP or ICMPv6 messages adds no security issue: over a connectionless lower layer such processing protects other nodes not supporting SCTP, but DTLS is a connection-oriented lower layer, so that protection is not needed. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Putting the two together creates no new dangers. SCTP just should not trust the sender addresses, because the envelope does not vouch for them.
